sampleChecks: shipment_latest holds 218 rows, one per shipment that has events (218 distinct shipment_ids). Nulls dataset: 109 rows. Ties dataset: 163 rows, where a shipment with two events at the same newest time keeps the event with the larger id (for example shipment 2 keeps event 4). The second run leaves the same rows.

rules.howSolved: DISTINCT ON (e.shipment_id) with ORDER BY e.occurred_at DESC keeps the newest shipment_events row for each shipment.
The secondary sort key e.id DESC picks the larger id when two events share the newest occurred_at.
ON CONFLICT (shipment_id) DO UPDATE lets the second INSERT update existing rows instead of failing on the primary key.
On the second run the upsert writes the same newest event for each shipment, so the table is unchanged.

runsTwiceCheck: The second run upserts each shipment's newest event with the same values, so no row changes and no error is raised. Checked on sample, nulls and ties: the state after run 2 equals the state after run 1 on all three.
ambiguities: 'shipment_id (integer, primary key, must name a shipment)' was read as PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES shipments (id).

The second run could update the existing rows (DO UPDATE) or leave them (DO NOTHING). The instructions do not say which. Both give the same state here; I chose DO UPDATE so the row always reflects the newest event.
notes: Run through PGlite on sample, nulls and ties: CREATE once, then the load twice, no errors. DISTINCT ON with ORDER BY occurred_at DESC, id DESC implements both the newest-event rule and the larger-id tie-break.
